prayerSequence.title: Prepare calmly
prayerSequence.body: Make wudu, find a clean spot, face the qibla, and settle in your heart which prayer this is. You do not have to say the intention out loud.

prayerSequence.title: Begin standing
prayerSequence.body: Raise your hands and say Allahu akbar. That opens the prayer, and from that point you have stepped out of ordinary talk and into worship.

prayerSequence.title: Recite in the first rak'ah
prayerSequence.body: Recite Al-Fatihah, then a short surah or the few verses you are working on. If you cannot recite yet, the section 'If you cannot recite Arabic yet' below explains what the schools allow in the meantime.

prayerSequence.title: Bow and rise
prayerSequence.body: Bow with your back flat and steady and say the bowing phrase. Rise while saying Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, and once you are standing straight say Rabbana wa lakal-hamd. Pause before you go down. Do not rush this to get it over with.

prayerSequence.title: Prostrate twice
prayerSequence.body: Go down into prostration and say the prostration phrase. Sit up and say Rabbighfir li, then prostrate a second time with the same phrase. Let each position settle before you move on.

prayerSequence.title: Repeat for the second rak'ah
prayerSequence.body: Stand again and repeat the same shape: Al-Fatiha, a short recitation, ruku, standing back up, then two prostrations.

prayerSequence.title: Sit for the final words
prayerSequence.body: After the second rak'ah, sit and recite the tashahhud. In a two-rak'ah prayer this is the final sitting, so add the blessings on the Prophet (salawat) before the salam. In a three or four rak'ah prayer this first sitting is shorter, and you stand again afterwards. The rak'ah map below shows where each sitting falls.

prayerSequence.title: End with salam
prayerSequence.body: Turn your head to the right, then the left, giving the greeting of peace each time. That ends the prayer. Sit for a moment before you get up and rejoin your day.

recitations.title: Opening takbir
recitations.beginnerNote: This is the first phrase to learn. Say it clearly and without hurrying. Your accent will come along on its own.

recitations.title: Al-Fatiha
recitations.arabic:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ
إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ
اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ
صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ
recitations.transliteration: Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim. Alhamdu lillahi Rabbil-'alamin. Ar-Rahmanir-Rahim. Maliki yawmid-din. Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Ihdinas-siratal-mustaqim. Siratal-ladhina an'amta 'alayhim ghayril-maghdubi 'alayhim wa lad-dallin.
recitations.meaning: Translation of meaning: praise, worship, and help belong to Allah, and we ask Him to guide us to the straight path.
recitations.beginnerNote: Al-Fatiha is the first real memorization goal. Take one phrase at a time, and ask a teacher what to recite while you are still learning it. In congregation, when the imam finishes Al-Fatihah and says Ameen (O Allah, answer), say Ameen with him. If you have questions about saying it when you pray alone, ask a teacher.

recitations.title: Short surah example: Al-Ikhlas
recitations.occasion: After Al-Fatiha in the first two rak'ahs
recitations.arabic:
قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ
اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ
لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ
وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ
recitations.transliteration: Qul huwa Allahu ahad. Allahus-samad. Lam yalid wa lam yulad. Wa lam yakun lahu kufuwan ahad.
recitations.meaning: Translation of meaning: Allah is One, self-sufficient, unlike creation, and nothing is comparable to Him.
recitations.beginnerNote: Most beginners start here. It is short, and it states the oneness of Allah in four lines.

recitations.title: Short surah example: Al-'Asr
recitations.occasion: After Al-Fatiha in the first two rak'ahs
recitations.arabic:
وَالْعَصْرِ
إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ
إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ
recitations.transliteration: Wal-'asr. Innal-insana lafi khusr. Illal-ladhina amanu wa 'amilus-salihat, wa tawasaw bil-haqqi wa tawasaw bis-sabr.
recitations.meaning: Translation of meaning: people are in loss except those who believe, do good, and encourage truth and patience.
recitations.beginnerNote: Work on one short surah at a time. Listening to a reliable reciter first does more for you than racing through several chapters.

recitations.title: Ruku phrase
recitations.meaning: Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great.
recitations.beginnerNote: Most guides teach saying this three times. While you are learning, one clear repetition is a fine place to start. Ask a teacher about the details.

recitations.title: Rising from bowing
recitations.arabic:
سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ
رَبَّنَا وَلَكَ الْحَمْدُ
recitations.transliteration: Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah. Rabbana wa lakal-hamd.
recitations.meaning: Allah hears the one who praises Him. Our Lord, and to You belongs all praise.
recitations.beginnerNote: Say the first line as you come up and the second once you are standing straight. You will also hear 'Rabbana lakal-hamd' without the 'wa'. Both wordings are in the hadith.

recitations.title: Sujud phrase
recitations.meaning: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.
recitations.beginnerNote: Sujud feels strange the first few times. Move at a speed your body is happy with, pause once you are down, and learn the phrase. Slow is not a failing.

recitations.title: Sitting between the two prostrations
recitations.occasion: Between the first and second sujud
recitations.beginnerNote: Two words, and the Prophet repeated them. Say it once or twice. A teacher can show you a longer version later if you want it.

recitations.title: Tashahhud
recitations.occasion: Every sitting: after the second rak'ah and at the end
recitations.arabic:
التَّحِيَّاتُ لِلَّهِ وَالصَّلَوَاتُ وَالطَّيِّبَاتُ
السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ
السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ
أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
recitations.transliteration: At-tahiyyatu lillahi was-salawatu wat-tayyibat. As-salamu 'alayka ayyuhan-Nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. As-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibadillahis-salihin. Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh.
recitations.meaning: All compliments, prayers and good things are for Allah. Peace be on you, O Prophet, and Allah's mercy and blessings. Peace be on us and on the righteous servants of Allah. I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.
recitations.beginnerNote: This is the wording narrated by Ibn Mas'ud. You may hear slightly different wordings from other authentic narrations, so follow your teacher. Learn it one line at a time.

recitations.title: Blessings on the Prophet (salawat)
recitations.arabic:
اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ
كَمَا صَلَّيْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ
إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
اللَّهُمَّ بَارِكْ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ
كَمَا بَارَكْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ
إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
recitations.transliteration: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammadin wa 'ala ali Muhammad, kama sallayta 'ala Ibrahima wa 'ala ali Ibrahim, innaka Hamidun Majid. Allahumma barik 'ala Muhammadin wa 'ala ali Muhammad, kama barakta 'ala Ibrahima wa 'ala ali Ibrahim, innaka Hamidun Majid.
recitations.meaning: O Allah, send Your mercy on Muhammad and on the family of Muhammad, as You sent Your mercy on Ibrahim and on the family of Ibrahim. You are Praiseworthy and Glorious. O Allah, send Your blessings on Muhammad and on the family of Muhammad, as You sent Your blessings on Ibrahim and on the family of Ibrahim. You are Praiseworthy and Glorious.
recitations.beginnerNote: Say it in the final sitting, after the tashahhud and before the salam. Whether it is also said in the first sitting of a longer prayer differs between schools, so ask your teacher.

recitations.title: Salam
recitations.meaning: Peace and Allah's mercy be upon you.
recitations.beginnerNote: This closes the prayer. Turn your head gently each way. There is no need to make a large movement of it.

cannotReciteYet: Keep praying while you learn. The scholars in the sources below say a new Muslim prays with what they can manage and learns the rest over time.

A widely taught option is to say short Arabic phrases of remembrance in place of the recitation: SubhanAllah (glory be to Allah), Alhamdulillah (praise be to Allah), La ilaha illallah (there is no god but Allah), Allahu akbar (Allah is the Greatest) and La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (there is no power or strength except with Allah). The Prophet taught these words to a man who said he could not memorise any Quran (Sunan Abi Dawud 832, graded Hasan by al-Albani).
SeekersGuidance calls these remembrance phrases the more cautious choice, because they are valid in both the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools.
The Hanafi school also accepts reciting a translation of the meaning for someone who cannot yet recite Arabic.
The Shafi'i school does not accept a translation. It allows a learner to read Al-Fatihah from a mushaf (a printed Quran) during the prayer.
The Maliki and Hanbali schools do not accept recitation in another language.
Reading from a book or screen during prayer is itself a point of difference: the Hanafi school counts holding a Quran and reading from it in prayer as prohibitively disliked (makruh tahriman).
In the meantime, learn Al-Fatihah one phrase at a time, then one short surah. Someone who recites with difficulty has two rewards (Sahih Muslim 798a).
Ask a local imam which of these options your community follows.
invalidatesPrayer: Losing wudu, such as by using the restroom or passing wind.
Eating, drinking, or speaking unrelated words on purpose during the prayer.
Leaving out a required posture, condition, or recitation once you know it is required.
Ending the prayer or turning away from it deliberately, with no reason to.
Mistakes, forgetfulness, illness, menstruation, travel, and disability all carry details worth going over with a qualified teacher.

commonCorrections.title: I keep restarting after every small mistake.
commonCorrections.body: Finish the prayer calmly, then ask about that specific mistake afterwards. The panic usually costs you more than the mistake did.

commonCorrections.title: I am embarrassed by my pronunciation.
commonCorrections.body: Pronunciation comes with repetition and nothing else. Allah knows the difference between someone who is not trying and someone who is still learning.

commonCorrections.title: Different videos show different hand positions.
commonCorrections.body: Those differences are usually all valid, and none of them are a reason to stop praying. Learn one reliable beginner method, and ask a teacher before you switch again.

commonCorrections.title: I rush because I feel awkward.
commonCorrections.body: Slow down until each posture is clearly its own. A short calm prayer teaches you more than a fast anxious one.

shapeImage.alt: Seven faceless figures showing one rak'ah in order: standing with hands raised, standing to recite, bowing, standing straight, prostrating, sitting, and prostrating again, each with its short phrase.
shapeImage.caption: One rak'ah, from the opening takbir to the second prostration.

items: Fajr, 2 rak'ahs: one sitting, after the second rak'ah. It is the final sitting: tashahhud, salawat, then salam.
Maghrib, 3 rak'ahs: a first sitting after the second rak'ah with the tashahhud, then stand for the third. The final sitting comes after the third: tashahhud, salawat, then salam.
Dhuhr, Asr and Isha, 4 rak'ahs: a first sitting after the second rak'ah with the tashahhud, then stand for the third and fourth. The final sitting comes after the fourth.
In the first two rak'ahs you recite Al-Fatihah and a short surah. In the third and fourth you recite Al-Fatihah only.

image.alt: A row of dots for each of the five prayers, one dot per rak'ah, with a sitting figure after the second rak'ah and at the end. Fajr has 2 dots, Dhuhr 4, Asr 4, Maghrib 3 and Isha 4.
image.caption: Where you sit for the tashahhud in each prayer.

sujudAlSahw.summary: If you forget part of the prayer, add something by mistake, or lose count of your rak'ahs, there is a simple repair: two extra prostrations called sujud al-sahw, the prostration of forgetfulness. For many mistakes you do not need to start the prayer again.
steps: If you are unsure how many rak'ahs you have prayed, go with the number you are sure of, which is the lower one, and finish the prayer from there.
Near the end of the prayer, make two extra prostrations with a short sitting between them, the same way you prostrate in every rak'ah.
Authentic reports mention these two prostrations both before and after the closing salam. The schools teach slightly different methods, so learn the one your teacher uses.
If you are praying behind an imam, follow the imam and do not add your own.
sujudAlSahw.referral: While you are new, finish calmly and ask a teacher about the specific mistake afterwards. Nobody expects you to know every rule in your first months.

rows.name: Dawn prayer (Fajr)
rows.window: From the first light of dawn until sunrise.

rows.name: Midday prayer (Dhuhr)
rows.window: From just after midday, once the sun has passed its highest point, until Asr begins.

rows.name: Afternoon prayer (Asr)
rows.window: From mid-afternoon until sunset. Try not to leave it until the sun turns yellow.

rows.name: Sunset prayer (Maghrib)
rows.window: From just after sunset until the twilight has gone.

rows.name: Night prayer (Isha)
rows.window: From when the twilight has gone until the middle of the night.

prayerTable.note: You can pray any time inside a window, so you do not need to be exact to the minute. Schools differ on when Asr begins (the Hanafi start is later) and on the latest time for Isha. In summer, much of Canada uses adjusted rules for Fajr and Isha, so use the prayer times page or your local masjid's timetable.

image.alt: A timeline of one day from dawn to night with the five prayers marked in order: Fajr at dawn, Dhuhr after midday, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib after sunset and Isha at night, each with its number of rak'ahs.
image.caption: The five prayers across one day. Exact times change daily with the sun.

notOwed.text: Prayers from the years before you became Muslim are not something you owe. The Prophet said that Islam wipes out what came before it, so you start from today. Some scholars add that a convert who did not yet know prayer was an obligation is not held to make up that time either. If you are unsure how this applies to you, ask a teacher.

seatedPrayer.summary: If pain, illness or disability makes standing, bowing or prostrating hard, pray in the way your body allows. The Prophet told a companion who was ill to pray standing, and if he could not, sitting, and if he could not, lying on his side.
points: If you cannot stand, or standing brings real pain or dizziness, pray sitting. You can sit on the floor, or on a chair if the floor is hard for you.

If you can still prostrate, the Hanafi answer we link prefers sitting on the floor and prostrating normally. If you cannot, lower your head instead: a little for bowing and a little further for prostration.
If you cannot sit, pray lying down, facing the qibla as best you can.
Short illnesses and long-term conditions are treated a little differently, and the schools differ on details such as how a chair user bows and where the chair goes in a row.
seatedPrayer.referral: A local imam or teacher can watch you pray once and help you settle on what works for your body. You never need to push through pain to make your prayer count. In hospital, pray in bed as you are able, and ask the nurses whether the hospital has a spiritual care team.

moreCards.title: Praying behind an imam (and joining late)
moreCards.summary: Walking into a masjid while the prayer is already under way happens to everyone. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said to come calmly, pray what you catch and complete what you missed (Sahih al-Bukhari 636).
points: Walk, do not run, and join the nearest row.
Stand, raise your hands and say Allahu akbar, then go straight into whatever position the imam is in, even if he is prostrating (Sunan Abi Dawud 893, graded Hasan by al-Albani).

If you bowed with the imam before he rose from bowing, you have caught that rak'ah. If you joined after that, follow him anyway, but that rak'ah does not count for you. The Hanafi and Shafi'i answers we link agree on this.
Move after the imam, never before him.
When the imam finishes Al-Fatihah, the people behind him say Ameen with him (Sahih al-Bukhari 780).

When the imam ends with salam and you still owe rak'ahs, do not say salam. Stand up and complete what you missed on your own. The Shafi'i answer we link recommends waiting until the imam has said both salams before you stand.
Stand close in the row, shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot (Sahih al-Bukhari 725). That is why the person beside you may move his foot next to yours.
If you make a mistake behind the imam, follow the imam and do not add your own prostrations of forgetfulness.
For your first few congregational prayers, stand near the end of a row where you can see people ahead of you. If you lose track, finish what you think is right and ask someone afterwards.
differences: What you recite behind the imam differs between the schools. Ask your teacher which way your community follows.

Catching Friday prayer: in the Hanafi answer we link, joining before the imam's final salam counts as catching Jumu'ah, and you then stand and make up two rak'ahs. The Shafi'i school counts Jumu'ah as caught only if you catch at least one rak'ah with the imam, and otherwise you pray Dhuhr. It relies on hadith such as "Whoever catches a rak'ah of Jumu'ah has caught it" (Sunan an-Nasa'i 1425, graded Sahih by Darussalam).

Two rak'ahs on arrival: the Prophet told people to pray two rak'ahs before sitting in a masjid (Sahih al-Bukhari 444). Once the imam goes up for the Friday sermon, the Hanafi and Maliki schools say not to pray, and to sit and listen. The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools teach two short rak'ahs even during the sermon, because the Prophet told a man who came in during the sermon to stand and pray two rak'ahs (Sahih Muslim 875c).
moreCards.referral: Ask a local imam to walk you through joining late once. It takes five minutes and saves a lot of worry.
